newsitem.title: RUSSIA: OECD sees Russian growth revival in 1997.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees Russian growth revival in 1997.

text.p: The Russian economy is likely to grow by two percent next year and five percent in 1998 as investment picks up and inflation stabilises, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said on Thursday.
A declining output trend had been expected to reverse this year but the OECD said in a semi-annual survey that gross domestic product was projected to fall four percent in 1996.
Almost every sector of industry experienced declines, although the shadow economy may have grown, the Paris-based think tank said.
"If the Russian government creates the conditions for private capital to flow into the economy, the recovery may finally occur," the OECD said.
It expects inflation to fall to 25 percent this year, 15 percent next year and 12 percent in 1998. Prices rose 131 percent in 1995.
Exports will grow slower in dollar terms in 1997, though trade with Commonwealth of Independent States members is growing.

The Russian current account deficit is forecast to be $1 billion in 1997, and $2 billion in 1998, after a $5 billion surplus this year, because of higher domestic demand and possibly some loss of export competitiveness.
Unemployment is likely to rise slightly to about 10 percent as the pace of restructuring increases.
Interest rates have been falling, though they remain rather high, and the banking sector remains fragile with a very large proportion of banks making losses, the outlook said.
It said Russia still faced tax collection problems, worsened by what it called improvised tax measures and tax offsets.
Wage and tax arrears have arisen as a result of unsustainable electoral promises and the rapid fall in inflation has jeopardised nominal tax revenues.
The OECD said a downward trend in Ukraine's economy may be close to bottoming out, with GDP projected to fall seven percent this year, after 12 percent in 1995.
Currency reforms, which introduced the hryvnia, were carried out successfully and trade flows have revived.
But output developments in the Baltic states have been disappointing, the OECD said.
"In Latvia and Lithuania this is mainly due to the recent serious banking crises," it says.

GDP growth of three percent in 1996 is expected in Estonia, the same as in 1995. Latvian output is seen growing 1.5 percent after a two percent decline in 1995 and Lithuanian growth will slow to 2.5 percent in 1996 from three percent.
Inflation is set to fall further to under 20 percent in 1996 in each of the Baltic states.
